speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Besides ensuring food safety, we also need to better regulate food labelling and advertising to promote public health and ensure that consumers get the right information to make informed choices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Today, we are seeing more innovative products entering the market, some of which are purported to give health benefits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Therefore, it is important for consumers to be provided with adequate and accurate information about the products they are consuming.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: In addition, the Competition Commission of Singapore (CCS)'s market inquiry into formula milk concluded that companies competed mainly on building a premium brand image for their products through aggressive marketing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: CCS also found that there is an insufficient understanding of the nutritional benefits of formula milk and the dietary requirements of infants and young children could have led some parents to perceive that the more expensive products were of higher quality.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: In May 2017, the Government formed a Taskforce, which I chair, to address some of these issues that were raised by CCS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The Taskforce has facilitated the entry of more affordable options, strengthened public education efforts and encouraged hospitals to provide more support for breastfeeding as the preferred option.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Parents have welcomed the positive impact of such measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Certain claims and images on tins create the impression, even when scientific evidence is weak, that these products can somehow do more for children.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: In this context, we are expanding the scope of the SOFA to regulate food labelling and the provision of information relating to food to help consumers make more informed choices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Coupled with education campaigns, we want to facilitate better understanding of products so that consumers do not, for example, always end up equating price or marketing claims with quality.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This will strengthen consumer protection, help consumers make more informed choices and promote public health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Second, clauses 9 and 19 provide a framework to better regulate the provision of information on food.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Currently, AVA regulates false labelling and advertising of food to prevent misleading claims.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: In the event that a case is brought to Court, the prosecution has to provide evidence of falsity to assert a breach.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The amendments will now require the defendant to produce evidence to show that the content of the advertisement or label is truthful.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: I should highlight that there is no presumption of guilt as cases still need to be argued before the Courts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Companies that can defend their claims will, therefore, not be unduly affected.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Beyond false advertising, we need to do more to safeguard consumer interest and promote public health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: In this regard, clause 19 clarifies the scope of regulations pertaining to the provision of information on food, for instance, specifying what can or must be contained in labels, promotions and advertisements, as well as how this content is being presented.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We already have a robust system that contributes to our reputation as a trusted and reliable jurisdiction when it comes to food safety.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: However, we are amending the Act to further enhance food safety, by allowing AVA to act more quickly on food recalls.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Currently, AVA stops the sale of food when it has been found, through testing, to be contaminated by food safety hazards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: However, food supply chains are becoming increasingly complex, given multiple sources, players and products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: It now takes more time to confirm the precise source and the nature of any contamination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This will prevent or reduce the possibility of serious danger to the public while investigations are still ongoing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: So far, our industry players have been responsible in taking quick remedial action when there are suspected cases and we are really grateful for their cooperation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: For example, in February 2016, some chocolate confectionery products were suspected to have been contaminated with pieces of plastic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: AVA was alerted to the incident via its scanning and worked with the importers to effect a recall.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: But this amendment will address future instances when there might be less responsible or cooperative industry players.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The amendment Bill also provides a recall framework that provides more clarity and certainty to the industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Clause 8 introduces a clear and gradated set of directions that AVA may issue to identified persons or entities for the purposes of food safety.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: If there is potential serious danger to public health, AVA may issue directions to recall food and food contact articles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: In less serious cases, directions can be given for general corrective actions or to control product movements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: AVA may also issue additional directions for follow-up actions, such as disposal, storage or publishing statements to the public.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Failure to comply with any of these directions will be an offence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We recognise that food recalls can cause reputational harm and disrupt business processes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Decisions to effect recalls are based on rigorous assessment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: AVA will also work with the industry to address situations before a food recall is announced.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: In the unlikely event of a false alarm, the Bill puts in place an appeal and compensation mechanism that the affected person or entity can use to seek redress.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The Bill also strengthens AVA's regulation of non-retail food businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The advent of new business practices makes this important.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: For example, third party logistics players are now providing space for businesses to store food and the storage conditions in some of these food warehouses are not ideal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: So, AVA has assessed that licensing food warehouses is a necessary measure to protect public health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: As for the other non-retail food establishments, AVA will study the need for licensing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Clause 6 makes clear the circumstances when the power to require information may be exercised by an authorised officer appointed by AVA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: For example, during investigations in the food poisoning cases, officers may ask for records like invoices, certificates issued by competent authorities or organisations, production records and so on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The amendment states clearly the circumstances under which authorised officers may exercise such powers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Clause 18 enables the Director-General of AVA to grant administrative exemptions for a specified period from any provisions of the Act or its subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: These exemptions are governed by strict criteria to safeguard public health and can only be granted to avoid unnecessary restrictions on trade.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: For example, this will allow AVA the flexibility to allow new brands or parallel imports even if they do not meet certain labelling requirements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: However, AVA will continue to ensure that these products still meet all the food safety standards and are safe for consumption.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We have already started consulting the food industry and will continue to engage and partner them throughout this transition.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We go to the greatest extent to enjoy our food.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But we are also a nation that is time-strapped, which means that we also rely heavily on processed foods.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The new regulations on food labelling will also help to demystify that cloud of misinformation that surfaces occasionally with fantastical claims on the properties of certain foods.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a parent myself, trying to understand the jargon on some infant-food items, it is perhaps more challenging than putting together a bicycle from scratch.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Having said that, I have a number of clarifications for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Much of the information on food products today and their nutrition or reported health benefits no longer occur at the shop fronts or on traditional advertising platforms.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many purchasers/consumers do their research online and this is where policing of misleading information may find its limits.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While a manufacturer may conform to standards required under our strengthened labelling regime, its claims online may paint a completely different story.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Labelling extends beyond just words as we now live in a very visual world.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A can of beans might just be a can of beans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But plonking a guy in a lab coat on a can and the advert suddenly makes the can, a can of super beans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The same has befallen the infant milk industry previously.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As parents, we naturally want the best for our children which makes us the perfect candidates to make rash but carefully considered choices after being bedazzled by the claims in infant food products.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: WHO international food standards already has guidelines discouraging mislabelling practices for infant milk formula, health claims and over-hyping nutritional values based on the purchasing psyche of parents.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Section 16(a) addresses this but I wish to seek clarity on how this policing can be achieved, as many of the claims that are stated by these products cannot be adequately tested or disproven.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Most of us think "fruit", and we think "healthy".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are juices and there are juice drinks and there are fruit cordials and there is nectar.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is an amazing number of different names for products when you go to a supermarket.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Foods gaze at you from the bottles or boxes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But hidden within them may be extremely high sugar content, preservatives and the confusing list of E-numbers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Truth be told, reported health benefits might be outweighed simply by the sugar content.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With regard to the recall of food items, I hope the Senior Minister of State can also update the House and the public on the current processes and how the new process will better guarantee food safety for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How often are tests done on imported food items and how much control is there, especially with the advent of online shopping?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The old adage of "buyer beware" may still hold true but the online shopping bonanza that has opened up means that individual consumers are also befuddled by the attractiveness of importing small quantities of food items, perhaps for their own consumption or to share with friends but which may be contravening AVA's guidelines or be extremely harmful.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For example, the recent instant hotpot recall is telling.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So much is being transacted online today that it will perhaps be very difficult for the agencies to be able to check every arriving parcel for food contraband.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How then will the agencies or the Ministry respond to the changing consumer landscape?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Notwithstanding the concerns I have raised, which I believe that the Ministry will address comprehensively, I support the amendments to the Bill.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I especially support clause 2 of the amendment's stated aim to "ensure the provision of information relating to food to enable consumers to make informed choices" and to prevent misleading conduct in connection with the sale of food.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I appreciate that the Act updates several definitions to bring it up to speed with the modern age of food and wellness bloggers, online shopping and multi-level marketing of alternative health and nutrition products.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The explanatory statement actually elaborates further that "this will make clear the situation where a food blog is published, or comments are made on social media, for no commercial gain to the blogger or commentator." I do not know how many young social media commentators and influencers are actually aware of the amendments being passed today.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But this broadened definition of "advertisement" does appear to cover posts on all the platforms they currently broadcast on.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Quite a few social media influencers are already doing paid or paid-in-kind posts for food brands.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And some have used their personal platforms to broadcast their clients' truth claims to their followers about food products.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Some of the less experienced young influencers may even post unedited, whatever benefits the client forwards them to say, believing that it is not their job or their place to question their paymaster.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Some years back, there was a small fuss kicked up online about how some young influencers were promoting a particular brand of processed juice.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: One influencer had suggested lightly that drinking juice was better than water any day.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And another used the #healthyliving while others made the truth claims that the juice was "fresh" and "high in vitamins".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: While it was clear to many commentators that drinking a litre of processed juice a day was probably not a good idea, what was less clear to many was whether an influencer's words should be shrugged off light-heartedly as private opinion or scrutinised critically as a professional piece of advertising designed to shift public choices.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Someone saying processed juice is part of healthy living may not seem like a big deal, but there are food and fashion influencers also crossing over into promoting food products created by the alternative health and wellness industry that makes far more ambitious truth claims.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I have seen bloggers push products that could help your "liver and circulatory system to return to optimal state", "neutralise free radicals" and the ever-popular promise to "reduce fats" or "eliminate toxins".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And pushing product through an individual's personal platforms seems to be a new place for brands to push their truth claims because of the greater leeway given to what appears to be personal opinion.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Some of our most successful young influencers under 35 have substantial followings.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: A 16-year-old micro-influencer in Singapore with a more moderate 10,000-20,000 followers may not pull in the same commercial rates, but can still receive paid-in-kind jobs because enough of their peer group perceive them as a legitimate source of information.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, such influence definitely has social impact and it seems they now could potentially bear legal responsibility.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: On behalf of online influencers and ordinary individuals who need more clarity about how this law relates to their food and wellness product-related social media posts, I would like to ask a set of questions.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: First, can I confirm what "commercial gain" to the food blogger, commentator or influencer means?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Second, the current understanding of many online influencers and their management companies is that the law does not require influencers to use terms such as "Sponsored Post" or "Advertorial" to flag that their personal posts are actually advertisements.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Third, some young people are getting into multi-level marketing of edible health and wellness products and are uncertain whether they would be construed as selling "food" by this Act.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: For example, therapeutic grade essential oils and essential oil-infused food and drink are a popular alternative health product despite the ongoing controversy in the United States of America about how this multi-billion dollar industry is being regulated.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This industry primarily sells through multi-level marketing and social networking.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: While the American Food and Drug Administration has worked with the parent essential oil companies to keep their product's promises within legal bounds, the FDA and parent companies have struggled to police the social media posts of the millions of independent distributors for non-compliant language, such as claims that daily consumption of essential oils can cure Ebola and cancer.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Can I clarify whether this definition would thus include any alternative health and nutrition products marketed as consumable, such as therapeutic-grade essential oils, detox teas and herbal shake powders?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, can I clarify: if an individual selling food products was simply reproducing the unedited health or nutritional truth claims passed on to them by a parent company or paying client, can they still be held personally accountable under this law should those claims turn out to be dubious or dangerous?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I also have a set of suggestions around the issue of food labelling.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Clause 19 expands the Minister's power to provide for regulations around food labelling.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And an example given in the explanatory notes to illustrate these new powers was, for the sake of combating obesity, retail food businesses could be required by regulations to disclose the energy or sugar content of the food that they sell and display this information in a clear, simple and unambiguous manner.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I am fully in support of the push for clear, simple and unambiguous labelling.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And many Singaporeans want to know what is actually in their food.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, I asked people online what kind of labelling they most want to see.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And here are the five big suggestions that are close to their hearts.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: First, to serve the rising number of people, especially children with serious allergies, allergens like nuts and seafood need to be highlighted and bolded.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This is especially for imported products where translations can be unclear, inaccurate and even leave out ingredients.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Second, fish and meat should state country of origin, whether they are farmed or wild, whether they use growth promotants, antibiotics or other synthetic colouring to enhance their appearance.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Few people are aware that a lot of cheap farmed salmon have their naturally grey meat tinted according to a colour swatch developed by a pharmaceutical MNC.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Meat products must also reveal how much meat goes into their composition.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, people should know which of the fast-food grilled chicken patties have actually less than 50% chicken and are mostly composed of cheaper fillers that could contain allergens.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Third, to prevent food waste, there should be one clear label to replace the confusion of "sell by", "packed by" and "used by" labels.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Clearer language needs to be used to distinguish when food changes in taste quality versus safety.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: A simple "Best if used by this date" and "Unsafe after this date" could be useful.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Fourth, serving sizes and measurement units used to help consumers compare nutritional data should be standardised, especially among locally produced goods, which are well within our control.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I found a local kaya bottle that said one teaspoon is 15 grammes while another local spread said one tablespoon was 15 grammes.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Standardised measurement becomes important, especially if we want to inform people about sugar content.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We need a simple, unambiguous label telling people exactly how much sugar, natural and added, is in their local and imported products.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If we use recognisable units like teaspoons and tablespoons rather than jargons like per serving or per gramme, more people can make meaningful comparisons.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Right now, not many people see that sugar content-wise, tablespoon for tablespoon, spreading chocolate hazelnut spread on our bread is actually the same as spreading on canned chocolate cake frosting.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: As a benchmark, powdered Milo has 45 grammes of sugar per 100 grammes and regular milk powder has 38 grammes of natural milk sugar per 100 grammes.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The formula tin said a 100 millilitres serving of prepared formula will contain 7.8 grammes of sugar.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: What appears to be a case of "I do not know why my child somehow likes the expensive formula milk better than regular milk" could turn out to be "my child likes sugared milk better than regular milk".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Fifth, I hope we can relook the design and wording of the Healthier Choice food label.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The Healthier Choice food label has been useful in influencing the supply side, encouraging companies to reformulate products according to the state's guidelines to produce relatively healthier products in each classified category.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But the key word here though is "relatively" and that is what is confusing a lot of people.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: People are writing to the press wondering how ice-creams, soft drinks, frozen french fries and highly sweetened yogurts, cereals and breads can bear the Healthier Choice label.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I have seen the Health Promotion Board's replies and I agree that there is no intrinsically good food and everything should be eaten in moderation.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: However, the term Healthier Choice itself is unambiguously a term that signals virtuosity and intrinsic goodness, especially because it only appears on some products and not others.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, when a child reads the phrase Healthier Choice, they naturally think, "Oh, it is healthier for me." They are unlikely to think, "Oh, it is healthier, but only relative to products in their same category and healthier because of certain ingredients but not others".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Even some adult shoppers I spoke to are unaware that there are tiny variations of qualifying text underneath the red Healthier Choice pyramid.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: An obtuse description like "this drink has 25% less sugar compared to regular soft drinks" is not that helpful.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I have found two groups of reactions to the Healthier Choice food label that are worth paying attention to.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: One, there are those who completely trust it and actively buy products with that label, believing it is an unambiguous rubber stamp of nutritional approval from the state.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I know several grandparents who let their grandkids drink multiple bottles of Healthier Choice-approved sweetened probiotic drinks, blackcurrant cordials and packaged chocolate malt drinks a day because of that.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And there are also those who are indifferent and even cynical of the label.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They argue that a sugary yoghurt boasting an absence of trans-fat, an artificially flavoured sweet white bread with a perfunctory addition of fibre and soft drinks using artificial sweeteners are undeserving of that label.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And I think they do have a point.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And there are many lessons, I think, we can learn from America's years of experimenting with providing better information as a solution to public health.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We have all tried eating healthy before, I am sure.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And even with great sources available to all of us, it has been a pain and a puzzle to figure out what is a better food choice.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Imagine how much more difficult it can be to commit to healthier eating if we were poor in either or all of these four domains of money, time, education and extra household help.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I hope, aside from just providing more information, we will continue to persevere and explore how to provide more practical support as well as accessible and affordable healthy food choices for the households who could really do with more help.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While nobody can quarrel with such aims, the amendments potentially allow AVA to impose onerous obligations on a wide variety of activities and businesses.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is a danger that the duties of compliance and the costs of compliance may kill off small businesses and community activities which pose relatively low risk to public health.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This Bill increases AVA's power over the current law in a few ways.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To summarise, the existing law is focused on enabling AVA to inspect places where food is sold, to take food samples for testing and imposing certain specific duties on those concerned with food establishments.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As the new Long Title states, the Bill now has a more general purpose of ensuring that food for sale is safe and suitable for human consumption and to promote public health and to ensure that the public have accurate information to make informed choices about food that is sold.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Compared to the existing law which focuses on punishing violations of baseline standards, the Bill now before the House is much more preventive and prescriptive.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This Bill casts AVA's net wide and installs AVA with new powers, especially in the proposed Part IIA of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While the new powers would be potentially useful in tackling errant businesses that produce or sell sub-standard food to the general public, it seems to me that other entities that provide useful services to segments of the public may potentially be subject to onerous requirements that are not commensurate with the risk.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A literal reading of the definition of "food business" will include the following types of activities: church fun fairs, which typically have stalls selling food and drinks; persons who host dinners or parties at their homes for a fee; a one-time private fund raiser which includes a meal; and traditional Chinese medicine shops, which also sell herbal tea eggs and herbal drinks.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We can all agree that such activities are worth preserving and they make an important contribution to Singapore's social and cultural depth.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under the new Part IIA, such activities would come under the new Food Safety Measures imposed by AVA.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: AVA will be empowered to give new directions to persons involved in food business activities to take preventive or corrective action in respect of food or a food contact article.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to the new section 10D, these actions to be taken include complying with specific steps to ensure the safety and suitability of food that is raised, cultivated, harvested, caught, prepared, sold or otherwise handled; taking specific steps to ensure that food premises, vehicles, food contact articles and equipment are cleaned, disinfected or altered; and to ensure that requirements of the Act are complied with.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: All these requirements are likely to be very specific, since the amended section 56 provides that the Minister will make regulations on these matters.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Section 10D further provides that until such corrective action is taken, the food business activity is to be suspended.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Besides section 10D, there are sections 10E, F and G which empower the AVA to impose controls over the movement of food, to recall food and to destroy and dispose of food.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Section 10H will require a Statement to be published by the person in charge of the activity, with information on any food that was recalled by AVA, the reasons for the recall and what remedy the person will provide.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Given that these are very draconian measures, will AVA devise a framework to differentiate between activities of high risk and activities of low risk and calibrate its regulatory response accordingly?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Recently, NEA informed them that they would need to obtain a foodshop licence; they also understand that they may have to undergo compulsory training as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is not clear what risks have emerged that necessitate more regulation of such shops.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are many such shops in HDB estates, where business volume may be moderate to low.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How burdensome will it be for food sellers to comply with stricter conditions from both NEA and AVA?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If AVA goes headlong into imposing onerous conditions on such businesses, some of them will find compliance difficult and too costly and may cease operations, to the detriment of their customers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for charitable and community initiatives which may be caught by the Bill, AVA should take an enabling and educational approach, rather than saddle them with costly and difficult requirements.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is a very interesting section that provides for the possibility of AVA paying compensation to a person who may have suffered loss as a result of AVA making a direction based on insufficient grounds.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I think the Minister earlier mentioned "false alarms".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, what if AVA relied on an expert report that turned out to be erroneous?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Another obvious question is: what kinds of losses would AVA recognise?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This Bill should not discourage community and charitable initiatives either.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It should also be borne in mind that if we are serious about encouraging and supporting entrepreneurship in Singapore, the Government should not impose excessive burdens and costs on small businesses.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is an important amendment Bill to strengthen our current Sale of Food Act, especially with new methods and platforms involving the sale of food, particularly, through online means.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Buying food is no longer about visiting a shop or stall that prepares the food, ordering your food, paying for it, then consuming it.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The food we order and eat now − whether we order from fixed premises or food establishments, or through online means − can come from many different sources, some of which we would never have fathomed of.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This neighbour was known to be preparing food items for a yong tau foo stall at a rather big food court.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Their domestic helper can be seen pushing trolleys of prepared food daily and even throwing the food waste into the dustbin at the void deck.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the residents of this block respect the enterprising spirit of their neighbour, they are concerned about two things: (a) the cleanliness and quality of the food prepared in the home of this neighbour, which is then delivered to the food court; and (b) the daily occurrence of raw food waste at the void deck dustbin, which has seemed to attract a bevy of rats to the block.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On a more personal note, about two months back, I purchased some pastries and cake from a rather established bakery chain.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When I sank my teeth into a chocolate cream puff, I tasted something slippery and plastic-like.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It turned out that it was a piece of sticky tape that had been churned in together with the chocolate cream.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I ended up throwing up and throwing away the cream puff.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am sure my experience is not unique as we have read of instances where inedible and unimaginable items end up in the food we eat − examples being plastic pieces, band-aids or even a rat.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are unpleasant encounters that we would never want happen on anyone.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that with the amendments proposed in this Bill, food stalls, food courts and members of the public, in general, will be more discerning in their choices of food suppliers and food sellers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would urge AVA to work with NEA to look into tightening the regulations and requirements for food handlers, food suppliers and food sellers to emphasise the need to have as much knowledge as possible about the handling, preparation and ingredients of the food they sell.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will help inspire confidence among consumers and will help weed out fly-by-night or rogue food operators who cannot care less about food safety and food hygiene.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Other than food ingredients, handling and preparation, I am also concerned about food items which claim to provide certain levels of nutrients or to even provide relief or cure from specific ailments.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, among the Malay community, Air Anugerah or bottled alkaline water sold at $2 per 500-millimetre bottle.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is claimed by the producers and sellers of this alkaline water that it "combines science and medicine to relieve pain spiritually and physically.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Alkaline water is known for hydrating the body while removing toxins, is an agent of anti-oxidants and able to neutralise acid in the bloodstream, leading to improved energy and oxygen levels".

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Air Anugerah is easily available for purchase online and I know of individuals who trust that this alkaline water will cure their ailments, more so than regular visits to their doctors for follow-up checks would.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am concerned about such food items that are sold online with regard to food safety and hygiene.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is difficult to regulate and monitor this entire segment of food item advertising and sale as there are numerous online platforms that do so, particularly where push advertising can be done very easily.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On the issue of consumer empowerment, I would like to raise some concerns over business practices that affect decision-making over food for the most vulnerable consumers − infants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that one of the objectives of the proposed amendments is to support initiatives of the Formula Milk Taskforce to tighten labelling requirements for infant formula.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One of the most vulnerable groups of consumers are infants in hospitals and they are protected by this Act since the expanded meaning of "sell" in section 2E does include "supplying of food in the course of providing services to patients in hospitals".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In hospitals, I understand that a rotation system is used to provide infants with milk formulas.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Majority of parents tend to continue with the brand of formula milk that their child was given in hospitals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Manufacturers provide sponsorship and/or payments to the private hospitals for participation in their milk rotation systems.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that majority of parents who use Formula Milk in hospitals do not have a preferred brand and tend not to switch brands of Formula Milk after leaving the hospital, manufacturers have invested significant efforts and resources into the marketing activities in the hospital channel to gain a ‘first-mover' advantage." Sir, I faced this problem when my babies were in hospital and, in the initial stages, Poppy had to be given some milk formula.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In my case, they were in a public hospital and not a private hospital.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My wife and I had a preferred brand of milk formula we wanted to give Poppy but were not allowed to.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We were told that we could use the brand that we wanted only when Poppy was discharged but were told that a switch in brand might affect the baby.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do understand that the Sale of Infant Foods Ethics Committee Singapore (SIFECS) under the Health Promotion Board is looking into this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we must bear in mind that they are looking to address this through reviewing its Code of Ethics on the Sale of Infant Foods in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, I would like to ask the Minister if the current proposed amendments to the Sale of Food Act could help to tackle this problem, too.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While we seek to make amendments to prohibit idealised images and health claims on infant formula labels and advertisements, these amendments become redundant when parents do not have a choice of which infant formula is given to their infants in some hospitals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such practices by manufacturers which are calculated to get infants "hooked" on their brands at an early stage and remove choices for parents to switch to cheaper alternatives seem to be contrary to the spirit of this Bill of empowering consumers in decision-making.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister clarify if the proposed expanded scope of the Sale of Food Act will allow it to address marketing and distribution practices by manufacturers and sellers that are intended to limit choices for particularly vulnerable groups of consumers?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also note that section 56 has been amended to allow any food regulation to incorporate any matter contained in any code.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, can the Minister also clarify if the Act will cover the sale of food online, as many Members have raised previously?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Even milk powder can be purchased online now and from outside of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I appreciate this is not an easy area to regulate but as there is a trend towards buying things online and from overseas, do we have plans to regulate this under the Sale of Food Act?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, Sir, I would like to seek clarification on the new section 55.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why is there a need to grant exemptions from the operations of all or any of the provisions of this Act or the food regulations?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State provide some scenarios as to when these exemptions are needed or necessary?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If there is really a need for such exemptions, may I suggest that a Board, which includes the Director-General rather than just one person, make the decision on granting the exemption?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So far, sellers have been given much leeway to exercise their creative licence in marketing their products.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Unfortunately, we have witnessed how harmful such practices can be and it is timely that the Ministry resumes a tighter rein on the information or misinformation which is provided to consumers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Does it mean that, in future, all food manufacturers and producers will be required to present evidence for the benefits claimed before their products can be sold in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How would we ascertain the reliability of such information?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For imported products, is there a list of accepted foreign bodies or government agencies which are certified authorities?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, I would like to ask if consumers will be allowed to take legal action against manufacturers for false claims.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In foreign markets, particularly the US, there had been such lawsuits in the past.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Ministry be able to support the affected consumers in prosecuting such sellers?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry share how would it ensure that the food recalled would not be recycled, repackaged or even re-exported for sale?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Do we have the manpower and expertise to conduct the necessary checks and investigations?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, I would like to conclude my support for the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Earlier this year, this House discussed infant formula prices in Singapore and the marketing practices of suppliers of infant milk formula.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Examples of misleading marketing claims used to justify high premium prices of infant milk powder were brought up and a taskforce was set up to look into such practices.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Minister's powers are expanded to provide for regulations which regulate the identification and labelling of food, including specifying the matter that must or must not be contained in labels and the manners of labelling.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the case of the infant formula market, we currently see indiscriminate use of labels marketing health claims and nutrition claims.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Health claims state or suggest that a relationship exists between a food or a constituent of that food and health, while nutrition claims suggest or imply a food has a nutritive property.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Consumers can be misled into paying premium prices for infant formula when supplies play to the psyche of parents wanting the best for their children and aggressively label certain minerals as supporting overall mental functioning, helping in physical development or development of the brain of the child.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Such labelling practices for infant milk formula are not allowed in many developed countries, such as Australia and New Zealand and also under the World Health Organization's (WHO) standards.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The selective playing up of certain nutritional elements in infant formula through labelling can also slant consumer purchasing decisions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I would thus like to seek clarification as to whether the current expansion of the Minister's powers to make food regulations extend to prohibiting health claims and nutrition claims on infant milk formula labels; and, if not, why.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What would be the associated regulations to regulate such behaviour?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Further, the new section 16(A) places the evidentiary burden on the defendant where failing to adduce evidence to the contrary where it is alleged that a person has made a false advertisement will result in the advertisement being found to be false.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Currently, there is only indirect protection against misleading advertising under the Consumer Protection Fair Trading Act (CPFTA).

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The CPFTA states that a consumer can only commence an action if he has entered into a transaction in reliance on a representation in the advertisement and damages cannot be claimed, unless he has suffered a loss as a result of reliance on the representation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For food products, and, in particular, for infant milk formula, this is almost impossible to execute as there is no way to prove that a child becomes less bright after the consumption of infant formula as compared to if the child had not consumed infant milk formula.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I, therefore, think that the amendment to the Sale of Food Act can play an important role in regulating misleading advertising.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lastly, I note that the amendment allows a new power to make food regulations requiring or regulating the display or distribution of nutritional information of a kind prescribed.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, as a means of combating obesity and to help people understand the implications of their purchasing decisions, proprietors of certain retail food businesses may be required by food regulations to disclose the energy or sugar content or food items they sell.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In our nationwide war on diabetes, this will certainly play an important role in promoting public health.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I believe that we all see the value in having better measures to enhance food safety and public health.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Having said that, Members have also expressed several important points which I will now address.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked how enforcement on claims will be carried out.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: He also asked if food companies will be required to present evidence about their product claims before their products can be sold in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There is already an existing framework for AVA to evaluate and approve health claims made on food labels and advertisements.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Health claims for food refer to any representation that states, suggests or even implies a relationship between a food product or its ingredients and health.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Examples of approved health claims are sentences and claims such as, "Calcium helps build strong bones and teeth" or statements, such as "Choline helps support overall mental functioning".

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Each time a company wants to make a new health claim, it has to submit an application to AVA with the relevant scientific evidence to back up the claims.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The claim is then assessed by AVA's Advisory Committee on Evaluation of Health Claims, which consists of members from academia, Government agencies and also from the food industry associations.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Committee evaluates these claims based on the principles recommended by Codex Alimentarius Commission.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is an international food standard-setting body that is established by the United Nations' Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) and the World Health Organization (WHO).

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: AVA will then review the Committee's evaluation to decide whether to approve that claim.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Once a particular health claim has been approved, any company may then use that claim on food labels and advertisements.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This process applies to both local and imported products.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In short, we already regulate health claims to a large extent.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh also asked if consumers will be allowed to take legal action against companies that make false claims.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The existing legislation already prohibits the use of false or misleading claims.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Consumers who have concerns regarding false or misleading claims on any of the food products can report these claims to AVA for their further investigation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Consumers may also commence an action against the company under the Consumer Protection (Fair Trading) Act, if they have entered into a transaction in reliance on these false claims made by a company and have suffered a loss as a result of the false claim.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Regulations can now be made to specify what claims are allowed and the manner in which they are presented.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, in other words, a claim need not be false for AVA to take action.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Any claim that negatively impacts consumers can be regulated, if necessary.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin made several suggestions on labelling.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Under the Food Regulations, all labels of pre-packaged food must indicate the presence of allergens or ingredients known to cause hypersensitivity, such as milk, eggs or nuts.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is to ensure that consumers with food allergies can make informed choices and avoid a medical emergency.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will study the other suggestions that she has raised.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Any claim that a product is 100% pure juice will have to meet prescribed standards.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin also asked about health products.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I would say these are separately regulated under the Health Products Act and have been explicitly excluded from this Bill.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin also made some comments about the Healthier Choice Symbol (HCS) programme.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As this programme is not covered under this Bill, we will pass her comments to MOH.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ms Sun Xueling asked whether the amendments will enable regulations to be made to prohibit health and nutrition claims on infant formula.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This will curb excessive marketing and improve clarity of labelling to ensure consumers can make informed choices.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We do not want parents to be unduly swayed into paying more for certain products due to aggressive or potentially misleading marketing.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Companies may then also end up passing on costs from these aggressive advertising and marketing activities to our consumers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Louis Ng has pointed out that some manufacturers have provided their products to hospitals and this could get infants "hooked" on to certain brands.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I understand Mr Louis Ng's concerns and agree that we should minimise brand lock-in at our hospitals.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In this regard, MOH has been working closely with both private and public hospitals to achieve the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI) certification.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: BFHI-certified hospitals must refuse gifts offered by milk companies and cannot distribute marketing materials or milk samples.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Currently, all three of our public hospitals with maternity services, namely, KK Women's and Children's Hospital, the National University Hospital and the Singapore General Hospital, are BFHI-certified and they have been certified for the last three to four years.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will continue to encourage greater uptake of this BFHI certification.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In public hospitals, the major brands of infant formula are rotated equally throughout the year.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is so that parents need not be "locked-in" to expensive brands of infant formula at a very early stage, especially during the post-partum period within the hospitals.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As for Mr Louis Ng's question on how the proposed amendments apply to this issue, the short answer is that they will enable us to regulate marketing practices in hospitals in order to promote public health and consumer interests.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: However, as explained, we are adopting a multi-prong approach to address this.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will assess the need for additional regulations, where necessary.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked whether the SIFECS Code can be incorporated into the Food Regulations.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This would give the Code some legal backing.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And these will be announced in due course.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But I must say that, on the issue of infant formula, it is not about just regulations per se.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We need to continue to step up public education so that our young parents are equipped with the correct information and knowledge to make the right choices because the asymmetry of information is what allows them to be exploited by aggressive marketing.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: With informed choices, our parents can then make the right choice of the type of formula that is suitable for their infants.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, for that, we must thank Health Promotion Board and MOH as well as grassroots organisations for conducting plenty of outreach activities in the community to reach out to our young parents.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Members have also made several comments about online and home-based food businesses.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Louis Ng and Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar asked if the Act would cover the sale of food online.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The current SOFA already allows AVA to regulate the sale of food, regardless of the manner in which they were sold.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: AVA will be able to take action against local agents, for example, the importer or distributor who makes the food available for sale through online platforms.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: However, consumers should exercise caution when purchasing food directly from overseas producers, including those from online sources, as their sources of distribution may not be regulated and AVA may not be able to subject the food to checks, if need be.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Alex Yam asked broadly about how AVA is responding to the changing consumer landscape in its regulation of the sale of food.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: AVA carries out its horizon scanning to provide early alerts of overseas food safety and animal disease incidents.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: AVA will assess these latest trends and developments and take appropriate measures to mitigate the risks to consumers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Alex Yam also asked about how misleading claims made by third-party advocates or influencers online can be addressed.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As I mentioned earlier, the amendments will allow AVA to regulate claims, including those made on local Internet sites.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This includes third-party advocates who have been paid to promote the sale of the product.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The onus will be on the local agents or the paid advocates to ensure that the claims that they are making are truthful.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin asked what constitutes commercial gain.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This could include monetary and in-kind sponsorships like freebies, gifts and discounts.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There is no specific law that requires a social media influencer to declare which of their personal posts selling foods have commercial interests.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: However, I think it stands to reason that a responsible influencer should also be a transparent one.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar's concerns are about the food safety standards and potential dis-amenity caused by home-based food businesses.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Residents are allowed to prepare small quantities of food for sale in their homes under the HDB's Home-Based Small Scale Business and URA's Home Business Scheme.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: NEA also does not regulate these businesses for food safety, unlike other food retail outlets.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That said, residents operating home-based food businesses are encouraged to adhere to NEA's guidelines on good hygiene practices and to attend NEA's Basic Food Hygiene Course.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Members of the public concerned about food safety or hygiene standards at these premises can contact NEA for further investigation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If the scale of such activity to conduct within HDB homes, for example, remains small, dis-amenity should be minimal.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But if the scale increases to an extent that creates inconveniences for neighbours, the business will then have to relocate to a proper food establishment.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, it is really a matter of scale and how much impact they have on overall public consumption and public safety.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Dr Intan 	Azura Mokhtar suggested tightening regulations to equip retail food business operators with requisite knowledge of good food safety and hygiene practices.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: All our food handlers working in NEA-licensed premises are already required to attend and pass the Basic Food Hygiene course and to attend regular refresher courses to equip them with the necessary knowledge and skills to guard against any hygiene lapses.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Food safety and hygiene are critical and this is why AVA and NEA will continue to work with our local food establishments to raise the bar on food safety and hygiene practices.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Alex Yam asked about how the new process for food recalls will enhance food safety.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Currently, AVA works with the industry to stop the sale of food when it has been found to be contaminated with food safety hazards.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: A test needs time to run and the results take time to be available.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is often better to take quick action to minimise continued risks to public health due to this suspected food contamination.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked how we would ensure that these recalled food items do not re-enter the food supply chain.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And if the products are meant for disposal, AVA officers will either personally witness the disposal, or allow the company to appoint authorised third-party disposal companies to do so.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: However, AVA may allow the recalled food to be returned to its country of origin, or be re-exported to a third country.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For the latter, re-export to a third country, AVA will require evidence from the importer to show that the authorities in the country will accept the products, even after knowing the reason why the products were not allowed for sale in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The importer will also have to engage an AVA-appointed security escort service to supervise the transport of the food to the port or checkpoint.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh also asked if AVA had the necessary expertise and manpower to oversee the entire food recall process.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As I have mentioned earlier, this process is not new and AVA has already been working closely with the industry for many years on such recalls.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked questions related to Part IIA of the amended Act.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As for her point on the reach of the new Part IIA, I need to clarify that these powers are discretionary.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They are only exercisable under certain circumstances as set out in the new sections 10D(1), 10E(1) and 10F(1).

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In all these cases, AVA must reasonably believe that there is non-compliance or hazard that poses public health risks.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This covers not only just food recalls, but any rectifications that are needed to ensure that unsafe food does not continue to be produced and distributed to consumers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That is why the provisions on food safety measures need to apply to a wide range of food businesses or any establishment that produces food for public consumption.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That said, these provisions will only be used when food safety lapses or issues are suspected, as I had said earlier.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As long as there are no food safety concerns, this should not present an impediment for food businesses or events where food is sold.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, if I may use the example that Ms Sylvia Lim quoted earlier about community events or, say, even a church event or a religious organisation giving out food, for example.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It really does not matter what entity it is, as long as food that is produced in that facility is being consumed by the public.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Just imagine a scenario where there is an outbreak of food poisoning.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If many people, after they have been to the event, have been admitted to the A&E while the event is still ongoing, I think the onus is on AVA to now make sure that there is compliance to immediately stop the distribution of food in that facility for further public consumption.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But, like I have said, this is only used in a time where there is a high suspicion or an actual incidence of food safety lapses.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In the absence of those, business as usual in all these events and places.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: AVA has rigorous Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) to identify food safety issues and to then deal with food recalls, food poisoning outbreaks, as well as follow-up actions that are necessary when food businesses are found to have produced contaminated food.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This SOP is regularly reviewed to ensure that it remains effective and current.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Any actions taken will be commensurate with the type of food-borne hazard that is suspected or detected, as well as the nature of the business itself.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For example, control measures can be calibrated according to the extent and severity of the case in question because no two incidents are similar in its nature.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In a severe case like when harmful bacteria or chemicals are detected in food, AVA can trigger a food recall and inform the public of this potential risk.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But in less serious cases, like the presence of just an unapproved food additive, for example, AVA can restrict the movement of the goods while it assesses the additive so it can halt the sales or distribution of food while the testing is underway.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is to ensure that the measures are imposed only to the extent that is necessary and to minimise business disruptions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And so far, for all the cases of food recalls that have taken place, there has always been close communication with the industry.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Many times, the industry players themselves would willingly want to recall the food items for fear of their own reputation risk of a persistent on-going food poisoning episode taking place in the community.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Hence, AVA will assess each case on its own merits to determine if the party claiming "insufficient grounds" has actually a case.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In the event that the party is dissatisfied with the decision, the party may apply to the Court for a review.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: At that time, L-theanine was not yet permitted for use as a food additive in Singapore, although it had been assessed to be safe by several countries which already allowed its use.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But because it was not gazetted at that time as a permitted food additive in Singapore, that product was not allowed for sale in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Hence, there was a certain delay and business cost.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The product was only subsequently allowed for sale after our legislation was amended.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Members would appreciate how much time it takes for legislation to be amended.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The point is, we want to allow some flexibility and not have to wait until legislation is amended in cases where there are no food safety concerns so that we can be pro-business while pro-public safety at the same time.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Director-General will also be supported by AVA's risk assessment team, which will thoroughly evaluate the food safety risks of any exemption, based on scientific evidence.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Any exemption made must also be publicised for transparency.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The proposed amendments to the Act are important in enhancing public food safety, protecting consumer interests and promoting public health.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: With evolving business landscapes and products, it is crucial that we continue to ensure that our legislation is both current and effective.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I have one clarification for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: This is in relation to Part IIA of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I think earlier on, he mentioned in his round-up speech that those directives will be given based on certain suspicion or information that there might be a non-compliance with the Act.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, it does seem to suggest that there may not necessarily be information relating to each particular case but the AVA could give directions to a class of persons who are running maybe a particular type of activity.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Further clarification for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I still do not quite understand how it ties.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Because the section says that the AVA is empowered to give particular directions to a class of persons.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: It could be persons running a particular food business or producing a particular food content article.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, it does seem to suggest that AVA could actually give preventive directions as a precaution rather than based on specific information about particular cases because it talks about giving directions to a class of people.
